Responsible‑AI Architecture Validation Report — PR #789 (CI: https://ci.example.com/builds/1402 ; signed build: https://artifacts.example.com/builds/signed_build_1402.tar.gz.sig)

Disposition: APPROVE WITH CONDITIONS. Quality & Security have implemented critical P0 mitigations (HSM-backed non-exportable signing keys, HSM-signed reports + verifier, single-use signed approval nonces + anti-replay store, safe_mode billing-gate, scheduler isolation & signed job manifests, immutable log forwarding, PII redaction, SBOM/depscan, reproducibility pipeline & fixed-point rounding docs). RAi accepts the architecture in principle but requires final evidentiary proofs and targeted operational tests (P0) listed below before issuing final approval. P1/P2 items must be scheduled with owners/SLA.

Assumptions
- The artifacts referenced by Security/Quality correspond to the deployed CI/build 1402 environment.
- Team assignment mapping exists for owners named below.

1) Focused validations mapped to provided evidence — required proofs, gaps, remediation, owner & priority
A. HSM / KMS & Key Ops
- Evidence present: HSM-backed non-exportable signing keys; key-access audit noted.
- Required P0 proofs:
  1) Non-exportability proof: KMS/HSM configuration export or attestation (console policy/screenshots + HSM attestation or KMS key policy showing non-exportable flag).
  2) Rotation/rollover runbook + recent rotation drill logs showing verification of existing signed reports after rollover or documented compatibility strategy for verifiers.
  3) Public-key distribution/trust model: endpoint or keyset publishing method (JWKS or signed public-key endpoint) and mechanism consumers use to pin/verify keys.
- If missing: enforce non-exportable keys in HSM, add rotation playbook and automated CI check to verify signatures post-rotation.
- Owner: Security/Infra. Priority: P0.

B. Approval flow & MFA (signed single-use nonces)
- Evidence present: signed single-use nonces + anti-replay store + MFA policy.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) Token spec: token format, cryptographic algorithm, binding to approver_id+report_id, TTL (<=5min recommended), and single-use enforcement mechanism.
  2) Anti-replay store design: HA/resiliency doc, retention/cleanup policy, replication semantics, and load/failover test logs proving no double-accept under failover.
  3) Enforcement evidence: integration test logs showing MFA enforcement at API gateway, service approval endpoint, and scheduler acceptance point; negative tests (attempt approval without MFA) demonstrating rejection.
  4) Bypass checks: explicit tests attempting alternate endpoints, direct scheduler calls, or CI-driven approvals that must fail.
- If missing: block upstream actions until token enforcement and anti-replay robustness demonstrated.
- Owner: Auth/Security. Priority: P0.

C. Billing‑gate / safe_mode
- Evidence present: safe_mode middleware with tests.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) Bypass-resistance tests: attempt direct DB updates to billing flags, attempt CI/automation to flip safe_mode, attempt scheduler-triggered billing; all must be blocked or require explicit approval flow. Provide test logs.
  2) Control-plane authority: evidence that the gate check is authoritative (service-level) and not only UI-level.
- If safe_mode is bypassable, remediate by moving gating logic into authoritative services and restricting toggle privileges to audited processes.
- Owner: SRE/Backend. Priority: P0.

D. Signing & Provenance (reports)
- Evidence present: HSM-signed reports + verifier lib.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) Signature algorithm and verifier tests: CI signature verification logs, tamper detection tests (alter payload -> verification fails), and a verifier library sanity check across environments.
  2) Provenance metadata presence: sample signed report with report_id, timestamp, input_hash (SHA256), generator_commit, env, SBOM_hash, rounding_policy_id. Show where metadata is stored and retrieval process.
  3) Rotation handling: procedure showing how verifiers handle key rollover (old keys still verifiable or transition policy).
- Owner: Security/Backend. Priority: P0.

E. RBAC & Privilege Escalation (BOLA)
- Evidence present: RBAC/gateway enforcement.
- Required P0/P1 proofs/tests:
  1) Role-matrix tests: positive/negative tests for revenue_viewer, revenue_approver, admin across API gateway, service, scheduler, management endpoints. Provide test logs.
  2) Object-level authorization tests to detect BOLA: tests where user A attempts to access/approve user B’s report must fail unless permitted.
- Remediation: add server-side object-level checks where gaps found; continuous RBAC tests.
- Owner: Auth/Security & AppSec. Priority: P0 for issues; P1 for coverage gaps.

F. Scheduler & Job Manifests
- Evidence present: scheduler isolation and signed job manifests.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) SA least-privilege evidence: IAM role manifests/policies for scheduler service account.
  2) Signed manifest enforcement: show that scheduler only runs signed manifests and that CI cannot inject unsigned jobs. Provide test log of attempted unsigned job rejection.
  3) Network egress controls: VPC/egress firewall configs. 4) DoS protection for scheduler: job rate-limits and quotas.
- Owner: SRE/Jobs & Platform. Priority: P0.

G. Audit / Immutable Logging & Non‑repudiation
- Evidence present: immutable log forwarding proof.
- Required P0/P1 proofs/tests:
  1) Immutable store evidence: configuration showing logs forwarded to append-only/WORM store and integrity checks (hash chaining or similar).
  2) Log contents: samples showing who/what/when/why (report_id, approver id, approval token id, key usage) with PII redacted; mapping showing how redaction preserves forensic utility (e.g., hashed customer id with salt stored separately in audited store).
  3) Alerting config: anomaly detection on approval/key access events.
- Owner: Observability/Security. Priority: P1 for config; P0 if immutability missing.

H. Secrets & CI Exposure
- Evidence present: signed builds and SBOM; Quality claims no secret leakage.
- Required P1 proofs/tests:
  1) CI secret-scan logs across artifacts/build logs proving no secrets leaked. 2) Build signing attestation and verification in deploy pipeline.
- Owner: Platform/Security. Priority: P1.

I. PII Protections & Provenance Privacy
- Evidence present: PII redaction and scans.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) Sample redacted report(s) showing input_hash and metadata but not raw PII. 2) PII classification schema and retention/deletion workflow with proof-of-deletion test. 3) Demonstration that provenance metadata cannot be used to re-identify data by unauthorized principals (e.g., hashed identifiers not reversible). If provenance requires linking to raw PII, show audited retrieval path.
- Owner: Data Compliance/Backend. Priority: P0.

J. Financial Calculation Integrity & Explainability
- Evidence present: fixed-point reproducibility tests and rounding docs.
- Required P0 proofs/tests:
  1) Reproducibility CI run logs covering rounding edge-cases (many small fractions, negative values, extremes), cross-architecture runs, and concurrency scenarios. 2) Calculation spec (human-readable) and a machine-readable calculation trace attached to sample reports (per-transaction contributions, rounding steps). 3) Property tests ensuring sum-of-parts invariants within declared tolerance.
- Owner: Engineering/QA. Priority: P0.

K. SBOM / Supply‑chain & DoS/Hardening
- Evidence present: SBOM v2 & depscan.
- Required P1 proofs/tests:
  1) SBOM remediation plan for any flagged dependencies and tracking items. 2) WAF ruleset, rate-limit/load test reports, and autoscaling behavior docs.
- Owner: Platform/Security & AppSec/SRE. Priority: P1.

2) AI/automation ethical risks & mitigations (owners & priority)
- Risk: Automated downstream actions (billing/collections) causing financial harm or disparate impact.
  - Mitigations: provenance token requirement for consumer actions; manual gating for actions above per-segment thresholds; staged rollout & rollback capabilities; audit logs of consumer actions. Owner: Product/Data Compliance (P0).
- Risk: Segment-level bias due to data quality/aggregation choices.
  - Mitigations: stratified stress tests, fairness regression gating, per-segment monitoring dashboards. Owner: Data Compliance/Engineering (P0).
- Risk: Re-identification via provenance or logs.
  - Mitigations: strong redaction/hashing policies; audited retrieval paths for full data; restrict provenance that embeds PII. Owner: Data Compliance (P0).
- Risk: Insider misuse (forged approvals, approval collusion).
  - Mitigations: MFA + single-use tokens, immutable logs, anomalous-approval alerts, periodic privileged access reviews. Owner: Auth/Security (P0).

3) Concrete test vectors & acceptance criteria (examples)
- Approval token replay: generate token -> consume -> replay => FAIL. Accept if replay rejected and logged.
- Approval token expiry: generate token TTL=30s -> use after TTL => FAIL.
- Forged token: modify signature/claims => FAIL.
- Tampered report: change report payload -> verification FAIL.
- Signature rotation: rotate key -> old signatures must verify per policy or be identifiable as legacy; new signatures validate.
- Reproducibility: archived_input + generator_commit -> rerun -> output == expected (bit-for-bit or within declared rounding tolerance). Must pass across two architectures or demonstrate deterministic guarantee.
- Safe_mode bypass: attempt DB write/CI toggle -> FAIL; evidence logs required.
- Nonce-store failover: simulate node failover during approval and ensure no double-accept; load test for expected throughput.
- PII leakage: run PII scanner -> zero unauthorized PII findings.
- RBAC matrix: every role test passes expected allow/deny matrix.
- CI secret leakage: secret-scan -> zero findings in artifacts/logs.

Acceptance criteria
- All P0 items must have passing automated test evidence or signed runbook logs attached to PR/CI for RAi to issue StopRai.
- Reproducibility tests for critical calculations must pass and be reproducible by auditors using archived inputs+generator_commit.
- Safe_mode bypass tests must demonstrate inability to bypass via DB/CI/APIs/scheduler.
- Signed report verification tests must run in CI and pass.

4) Monitoring & alerting rules, thresholds & SLAs
- Must implement: signature verification failure => Pager (P0). Reproducibility CI failure => Pager (P0). Nonce replay attempts > 0 => Pager (P0) + freeze affected account. Any automated downstream action beyond high_impact_threshold without approval token => automatic rollback + Pager (P0). PII scanner positive in production => Pager (P0). Approval step-up failures per approver > 5/hr => Security review (P1). Per-segment delta > Y% => quarantine + triage SLA: 4 hours; full review SLA: 48 hours.

5) Minimal viable mitigations (blocking) and explicit RAi blockers
- Given Quality’s P0 fixes, RAi-blocking items are now evidence/test-based. RAi-blockers (must be provided/proved before final sign-off):
  1) HSM non-exportability proof + rotation drill evidence (P0).
  2) Anti-replay nonce-store correctness & failover/scale test logs (P0).
  3) Enforcement proof for single-use, MFA-bound approval tokens at gateway/service/scheduler and bypass-resistance tests (P0).
  4) Safe_mode bypass tests proving no DB/CI/API/scheduler bypass (P0).
  5) Reproducibility CI runs including rounding-edge coverage (P0).
  6) PII redaction evidence with provenance preservation plus PII-scan results (P0).

6) Deliverables required (attach to PR/CI build 1402)
- KMS/HSM non-exportability config & rotation drill logs.
- Nonce-store design doc + HA/scale/failover test logs.
- Approval-flow token spec + enforcement logs (MFA enforced at all points) + bypass test logs.

- Sample signed report(s) + CI verifier logs + key rotation handling doc.
- Reproducibility CI job outputs including rounding edge-case tests and cross-arch runs.

- Immutable log forwarding proof and alert config.
- SBOM v2 and dependency remediation plan; signed build attestations.

payload:
Responsible-AI review for PR#342 (Add /api/revenue and RevenueService)

Summary / immediate question
- I do not see in the PR whether RevenueService performs any ML/heuristic inference or only deterministic business logic. Please confirm explicitly: (A) Is any model, heuristic scoring, or predictive inference used now or planned? If yes, identify model name(s), inputs, outputs, and owners. If no, confirm revenue values are purely transactional/derived arithmetic.

If ML/Inference is used (requirements)
- Model governance: require model registry entry and a Model Card that documents training data sources, intended use, inputs/outputs, limitations, owners, and model versioning. 
- Data lineage & training data: provide provenance for training/label data, access controls for those datasets, and a retention policy. 
- Validation & testing: offline validation results (accuracy/perf metrics, confusion matrices, calibration, and fairness metrics) and threshold gating for deployment. Include unit and integration tests for edge cases. 
- Explainability: provide per-inference explainability approach (SHAP/feature importance or rule tracing) for high-impact decisions or where explainability is required by policy/regulation. 
- Monitoring & CI/CD: continuous monitoring for drift, performance regression, and concept shift; automatic rollback triggers if metrics cross thresholds. Include retraining process and a reproducible retraining pipeline. 

Privacy / PII assessment and controls
- Required: deliver a field-level data map for all fields written to indices and returned by /api/revenue (names, types, whether they are PII/sensitive, and retention TTL).
- Minimize: do not store direct identifiers (name, email, SSN). If identifiers are required for business reasons, store only pseudonymized values (HMAC or keyed hashing with rotation policy) and store keys separately with strict KMS access controls.
- Anonymization: for analytic indices, use aggregated or bucketed values where possible; consider differential privacy for aggregated exports if the dataset is small.
- Retention: define and enforce explicit retention windows per data class (e.g., transaction records: X days/years; derived scores: Y days) with automated deletion jobs and demonstrable logs. 
- Consent / DSRs: ensure mechanisms for Data Subject Requests (access/erasure) that can remove or pseudonymize data across indices and backups. Document consent basis for storing and processing revenue data.

Sensitive inferences / profiling risk
- Evaluate whether RevenueService or downstream consumers could infer sensitive attributes (e.g., income bracket, creditworthiness). If so:
  - Avoid storing raw attributes that enable sensitive inferences when unnecessary.
  - Apply aggregation thresholds (k-anonymity style) for reports or require differential privacy.
  - Add manual review or human-in-the-loop for high-risk outputs (decisions that affect users materially).

Access control & ownership
- Least privilege: RBAC roles for human and service access. Example roles: revenue-reader (readonly), revenue-writer (service), revenue-admin (schema/manage). No broad admin roles without justification.
- Service-to-service auth: require mutual TLS and short-lived mTLS/JWT tokens (service identity via SPIFFE/SVID or internal identity provider). Avoid static API keys.
- Multi-tenant isolation: if indices contain multi-tenant data, enforce tenant-id scoping at the storage and query layer and validate authorization server-side. Consider separate indices per tenant if required by policy/regulation.
- Owners/approvals: assign a data owner and a schema owner for the new indices; these owners must sign off on retention, access policies, and backups. Security and Arch should be listed as approvers for the index ownership.

Logging & observability
- Log what: request metadata (timestamp, non-PII request shape, response status, latency), access authorizations (who/which service), and model/inference IDs when applicable.
- Redact/avoid: never log PII/sensitive attributes or persist them in plaintext in logs. Mask or hash identifiers before logging. Metrics should be aggregated and non-identifying.
- Retention/rotation: align log retention with privacy policy and audit needs; keep access logs sufficiently long for audits but avoid indefinite retention. Implement log rotation and secure storage; restrict access to logs containing pseudonymized identifiers.
- Audit trails: log all schema changes, data exports, model deployments, and privileged data accesses. Ensure logs are immutable and monitored.

Monitoring for misuse and model drift
- Misuse detection: anomalous access patterns, elevated request rates from a single actor, unusual query shapes, or bulk-export attempts. Alert on privilege escalations and on high-volume reads of sensitive indices.
- Model drift signals: data distribution change (covariate shift), label distribution change, sudden degradation of performance metrics, increase in downstream complaint rates. Define thresholds and alerting for each metric.
- Response strategy: automated throttling/quarantine of offending client, ability to disable predictions (feature flag), automatic rollback to previous model, and human review process. Include runbooks for investigation and remediation.

Required Responsible-AI documentation & approvals before deploy
- If ML/inference: Model Card, training data lineage, validation report, fairness audit (if decisions affect users materially), and risk register entry.
- Privacy: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) if personal data is processed at scale or sensitive inferences can be made. Document DSR handling procedures.
- Sign-offs: Responsible-AI reviewer (me), Data Protection Officer / Privacy team, SecurityReviewer, and ArchReviewer must sign off on the above artifacts.

Concrete technical constraints and controls (actionable)
1) Data classification: produce a schema with classification (PII/sensitive/non-PII) before merge. Blocker until provided.
2) No PII in logs or returned payloads. Implement automatic redaction at service boundary and validate via tests. Blocker.
3) S2S auth: require mTLS + short-lived JWT; no plaintext credentials. Implement and test. Blocker.
4) RBAC: define roles and apply least-privilege. Ensure service accounts only have write access if needed and read-only tooling accounts limited. Blocker for prod push.
5) Retention & deletion: implement TTL enforcement for indices and a documented deletion job with audit logs. Blocker until retention policy exists.
6) Rate limiting/abuse: add per-client and per-service rate limits; instrument alerts for spikes. Recommend Security coordinate limits.
7) If ML used: model registry entry, automated model CI/CD gating, drift detection, and rollback mechanism. Blocker for any model-inference deployment.
8) Tenant isolation: if multi-tenant, enforce tenant-scoped queries at API layer and verify with tests. Blocker if not demonstrated.

Blocking concerns (must be resolved before I can clear Responsible-AI)
- Unclear whether ML/prediction is used; if so, no model governance artifacts are present in PR.
- No field-level data map / PII classification for index fields or endpoint payloads provided.
- No explicit access-control plan (RBAC roles, service auth) or index owner specified.
- No retention policy or DSR handling described.
- Logging policy unclear about PII redaction.

Next steps for author/Arch/Security
- Provide answers to the immediate question (ML used? list models) and attach the schema with PII flags.
- Produce or reference model governance artifacts if models are used; otherwise state explicitly that the service is deterministic.
- Add or reference retention policy, index owner, RBAC roles, and S2S auth mechanism in the PR description.
- Add tests demonstrating PII redaction in logs and tenant-scoped access.

If the above items are resolved and artifacts are attached, I will re-review; until then this Responsible-AI review is a conditional approval pending closure of the blocking items above.

label: ToMerger
payload:
Responsible-AI review (PR#342 — revised): summary, concrete controls, and blockers

High-level conclusion
- Arch's revision states RevenueService is deterministic aggregation only (NO ML). Based on the provided artifacts (field_data_map, DPIA (low-risk), retention/deletion job, DSR flow, KMS-backed HMAC pseudonyms, RBAC tests, tenant isolation, logging redaction tests, rate-limiting, migrations, sample data) I provisionally accept that no ML/inference is present. However, I require an explicit, signed developer attestation in the PR that: (a) there is zero ML/heuristic/inference code in this change set or migrations, and (b) no models or derived-score pipelines are referenced by downstream consumers. This attestation plus an automated CI check for model artifacts (e.g., no model files, no model registry references) is required before final sign-off.

1) Absolute ML confirmation & future governance
- Action: author must add an explicit signed statement in PR description: “No ML/heuristics/inference in code, migrations, or downstream manifests for this change.”
- If any future derived-prediction features are planned, they must follow model governance: model registry entry, Model Card, training-data lineage, validation reports, fairness audit, CI gating, drift monitoring, and rollback mechanisms (see earlier checklist). Deploying any model without these is a blocking violation.

2) Re-identification risk for monthly deterministic aggregations
- Minimum cell size: require suppression for any aggregation cell with count < 10. Where counts are < 10, suppress the cell or return an aggregated bucket.
- Rounding/suppression: apply deterministic rounding for numeric aggregates (e.g., round dollar aggregates to nearest $10 or bucket into income brackets) to reduce exact-value leakage.
- If small populations are expected (rare tenants or low-volume slices), require additional aggregation or suppression thresholds or apply differential-privacy mechanisms before release.
- Action: author must document how aggregation queries enforce the min-cell-size check and include unit tests that exercise small-cell behavior. Blocking until tests exist.

3) Pseudonymization & keying (KMS-backed HMAC)
- KMS usage: acceptable as core control. Required additional controls:
  - Per-environment keys (dev/stage/prod) and no key reuse across environments.
  - Per-tenant HMAC salts/derived keys where feasible to reduce cross-tenant linkage risk.
  - Key rotation cadence: rotate signing/HMAC keys every 90 days by default; emergency rotation playbook must exist.
  - Separation of duties: key creation/rotation is performed only by ops/security roles; application code cannot export plaintext keys.
  - Access controls: HMAC verification must be performed server-side; raw identifiers must never be stored in plaintext in indices or logs.
- HMAC alone reduces but does not eliminate linkage risk (especially if same HMACed identifier appears in multiple datasets). Recommend per-tenant salts and limited retention of pseudonyms if cross-index linkage is a concern.

4) DPIA validation
- DPIA marked low-risk is acceptable if no sensitive inference and if retention/controls are implemented as claimed.
- Escalate DPIA/legal if: revenue aggregation could be used to profile income/creditworthiness, or if small-tenant datasets permit re-identification despite pseudonymization. Action: privacy office must sign final DPIA closure evidencing review of aggregation thresholds and retention.

5) Data minimization & outputs
- API returns MUST be limited to aggregate metrics only (no direct identifiers, no raw transaction rows). Remove any sample fields in sample data that contain identifiers; store only HMACed IDs where needed.
- For numeric revenue values exposed externally, apply bucketing or rounding where high precision is unnecessary.
- Action: update sample responses in PR to show only final allowed fields and include tests verifying that endpoint never returns PII.

6) Logging & telemetry
- Allowed logs: timestamp, request route, non-PII request parameters (e.g., tenant_id if pseudonymized), response status, latency, service principal identity, model/inference id (not applicable here), and query aggregation keys (only when not PII or already pseudonymized).
- Redact/avoid: do not log raw identifiers (email, name, account number) or exact revenue values tied to single-user records. Mask HMACed IDs when logged unless logs are access-controlled and necessary for debugging (prefer pseudonym hashes rather than raw HMAC values in logs).
- Required audit fields: actor (service or user id), timestamp, action (read/write/index migration), query parameters (redacted), result size, and authorization decision.
- Retention policy: detailed access logs — retain for 90 days by default; audit logs required for compliance — keep for up to 365 days if justified by audit/legal needs. Aggregated metrics can be retained longer (e.g., 2+ years) but must be non-identifying.
- Action: confirm retention intervals in PR and add automated log-redaction tests (already provided — reviewer to validate test coverage).

7) Multi-tenant isolation
- Design confirmation: separate index namespaces per tenant preferred. If using shared indices, enforce tenant-scoped queries at the API and storage layer with strong authorization checks in code and tests.
- Cryptographic separation: use per-tenant salts/keys for pseudonymization to prevent cross-tenant linkage.
- Action: author must show tests that attempt cross-tenant access and validate denial; blocking until those tests pass.

8) Migration risk & rollout
- Safe rollout approach: use shadow indexing/backfill approach; create new indices and populate them in parallel, run canary queries against shadow index, validate results, then switch read traffic to new index.
- Backfill window and verification: ensure backfill job runs with minimized privileges and that temporary storage does not include raw identifiers unprotected. Any temporary mapping that could expose PII must be encrypted and access-controlled.
- Rollback: ability to revert to previous index mapping and delete shadow indices if anomalies detected.
- Action: require migration plan in PR showing shadow/canary steps and verification checklist. Blocker until plan present and includes no-exposure guarantee.

9) Monitoring for misuse and scraping risk
- Detection signals: unusually high request volume from a single principal; many small-aggregate queries that could be combined to reconstruct individuals; repeated queries with varying filters that converge on tiny populations; cross-tenant access attempts.
- Alerts & thresholds: recommend gateway-level rate limits + application-level throttles. Example starting thresholds: per-tenant 60 requests/min, per-client 30 requests/min, adjustable by capacity and business need. Enforce burst limits and slow-down backoff. (These numeric defaults are a starting point; Security/Arch should finalize.)
- Automated mitigations: temporarily throttle/quarantine offending principal, require manual review for repeated offenses, and automatic temporary blocking for suspected scraping.
- Action: show test cases and monitoring dashboards in PR; blocking until detection alerts are wired and tested.

10) Documentation & sign-offs required pre-deploy
- Required artifacts before deployment:
  - Final DPIA signed by Privacy team (if not already fully closed).
  - Responsible-AI sign-off (this reviewer) after closure of blockers.
  - Security sign-off (SEC-123) verifying auth, rate-limiting, and migration security.
  - Arch sign-off (ARCH-77) on service-mesh placement and index ownership.
  - Data owner and schema owner named in PR with documented responsibilities.
  - Tests: CI tests for PII redaction in logs, tenant isolation tests, min-cell-size suppression tests, and migration canary tests.

Concrete numeric/operational constraints (must be enforced)
- Minimum cell size for release/summaries: N = 10 (suppress or aggregate below this).
- HMAC key rotation: every 90 days; per-environment/dev/prod key separation mandatory.
- Log retention: detailed access logs — 90 days; immutable audit logs — up to 365 days (document justification if longer).
- Rate-limiting: gateway-level initial defaults (per-tenant 60 req/min, per-client 30 req/min); must be configurable.
- Retention enforcement: TTL on indices with automated deletion job (as provided); retention periods must be declared per field/class in the field_data_map.

Blocking concerns (must be resolved before Responsible-AI clears PR)
1) Signed developer attestation of NO ML/inference plus CI check to prevent accidental ML artifacts. (Blocker)
2) Proof/tests that aggregation enforces min-cell-size suppression (N=10) and numeric rounding/bucketing are applied where needed. (Blocker)
3) Key management evidence: per-environment keys, per-tenant salts (if feasible), rotation policy and separation-of-duties. (Blocker)
4) Migration plan showing shadow index/canary/backout steps and evidence that no PII is exposed during migration. (Blocker)
5) Monitoring/alerting wiring and tests for misuse/scraping detection. (Blocker)
6) Final DPIA sign-off by Privacy if any risk remains for sensitive inference or profiling. (Blocker until signed)
7) Confirmed RBAC mapping in deployment config and tests proving tenant isolation. (Blocker)

If the above blockers are cleared (artifacts uploaded to PR and tests passing), I will remove the Responsible-AI block and sign off. Otherwise this review remains a conditional approval pending closure of these concrete items.

- HMAC key rotation: every 90 days; per-environment key separation (dev/stage/prod) mandatory.

Responsible-AI assessment and conditional sign-off for PR#342 (final revision)

Short answer
- I can provisionally sign off Responsible‑AI on PR#342 provided the concrete blockers below are closed with artifacts. Most technical controls are acceptable in principle (no ML in the change set, per-tenant & per-env KMS-backed HMAC, N=10 suppression + rounding, encrypted shadow indices, tenant-isolation tests, logging redaction tests, retention/deletion jobs, CI gating, monitoring/runbooks). However several final proof‑points must be delivered before I issue a final sign-off.

Decisions & concrete constraints
1) ML/inference
- Condition: I accept there is no ML/inference in this PR only after an explicit signed developer attestation is added to the PR description: “No ML/heuristics/inference code in this change set, migrations, or downstream manifests.”
- CI requirement: add a CI scan/artifact proving no model files or model-registry references; link CI run in PR.

2) Re-identification & suppression thresholds
- Baseline: Min cell-size = 10 with deterministic rounding to nearest $10 is acceptable only for low-sensitivity monthly aggregates where the tenant population > 100 and returned dimensions are limited.
- If tenant population <= 100 or if attributes are high-sensitivity (income/credit profiling), raise min cell-size to >= 20 (recommended) or >= 50 for high-sensitivity cases.
- Additional controls: enforce combination-level suppression (if any multi-dim group-by produces a cell < threshold, suppress) and limit dimensionality of allowed queries (max group-by dimensions per query).
- Alternative (stronger): for externally published reports consider DP; if DP used target epsilon <= 1 (delta <= 1e-5) and document privacy budget management.

3) Pseudonymization & keying
- Approved design: per-tenant & per-environment KMS-backed HMAC-SHA256 with separation-of-duties and 90-day rotation is acceptable.
- Required: prove per-tenant salt/key usage (or provide threat-model justification if per-tenant keys not used). Must show dev/stage/prod key separation and that app code cannot export plaintext keys.
- Key audit: provide key-access audit logs (who/when) and show SoD controls; rotation playbook must be attached.
- Optional: consider truncation or prefix-hiding of HMAC outputs if linkability across external systems is a practical risk—only after verifying collision risk is acceptable.

4) DPIA / legal basis
- PRIV-55 and LEG-89 appear to be provided. Provide explicit DPO/privacy sign-off artifact (signed closure) linked in PR. If DPO flags residual risks (e.g., small-tenant re-id), follow escalation steps.

5) Data minimization & retention

- Must redact PII from logs; allowed audit fields: who (actor/service id), what (action/read/write/migration), when (timestamp), why/request-id, query parameters (redacted), and result size (aggregate after suppression).
- Retention: recommend immutable audit logs retained at least 1 year; access logs 90 days by default. For regulated customers increase to 3+ years as required by compliance — show justification if longer.
- Provide evidence: log-redaction test outputs and retention config in PR/CI.

7) Multi-tenant isolation & index design
- If shared indices used, require per-tenant salts/keys and tenant-scoped authorization enforced in API and storage (tests required). If high-risk tenants or regulatory constraints exist, use per-tenant indices.
- Provide tenant-isolation test results (already referenced) and attach test artifacts to PR.

- Safe rollout required: encrypted shadow indices, canary queries, automated verification of suppression/min-cell-size after backfill, and automated revert criteria in runbook.
- Provide canary verification outputs and show that temporary artifacts never contain plaintext identifiers unencrypted.

9) Misuse detection & enforcement point

Decision: BLOCK (pending exact guardrails & proofs for dynamic suppression)

Summary

This is a good implementation direction, but before Responsible‑AI can sign off I require a small number of concrete guardrails, configuration placements, approvals, and test/proof artifacts. I list exact blocking items and required remediation below.

Blocking items (exact remediation required)
1) Global minima & tenant rules (MUST): implement and document a global floor and population/sensitivity rules in suppression_policy.yaml and enforce them at runtime. Required concrete values:
   - Global floor (cannot be overridden downward): global_min = 10.
   - Tenant population rule: if tenant_population <= 100 then effective_min >= 20.
   - High‑sensitivity attributes rule: any aggregation involving flagged high‑sensitivity attributes must use effective_min >= 50.
   - Enforcement: policy engine must compute effective_min per request and never return cells below effective_min.
   - Provide unit & integration tests proving enforcement for these exact values.

2) Overrides: forbid unsafe reductions & require approvals (MUST)
   - Overrides are allowed only to increase suppression (make stricter) by default.
   - Any override that would reduce effective_min below the computed rule (from item 1) is forbidden unless two approvals are recorded: Data Owner + Privacy (DPO). Dual approval must be captured as an approval_id in the override audit record.
   - Overrides must not reduce below global_min = 10 under any circumstances.
   - Provide an approvals workflow spec and tests that attempt forbidden overrides and verify rejection; attach sample approved override records in PR.

3) Policy storage & RBAC (MUST)
   - Default policy may live in repo as defaults, but per‑tenant overrides MUST be stored in the secure config service (not plaintext in general repo) or in an encrypted/sealed store with strict RBAC.
   - Only a small set of roles (ops_security, data_owner, privacy) may modify overrides; record all changes immutably.
   - If infra/configs/suppression_policy.yaml remains in the repo, it must contain only defaults; per‑tenant override file(s) must be in secure config with change approval gating.
   - Provide an access-control matrix and show that CI gating enforces protected-branch PR approval for any default change.

4) Override audit logging & retention (MUST)
   - Audit log entry for any override must include: actor id, role, justification text, approval ids, timestamp, old_value, new_value, request_id, and link to approval artifacts.
   - Audit logs must be immutable and retained at least 7 years (current infra claims 7y; confirm retention and immutability in PR). Attach sample immutable log entry from staging run (run 12355).

5) Re‑identification simulation & gating (MUST when override reduces protection)
   - Any attempt to lower suppression relative to the computed effective_min (even temporarily) requires a re‑id simulation report (automated test) demonstrating acceptable risk (attach simulation outputs). If simulation not passed, deny override.
   - Provide a definition of the acceptance test (metrics e.g., uniqueness rate, risk score threshold) and at least one passing simulation for a representative override (attach to PR).

6) Runtime enforcement locus & ordering (MUST)
   - Suppression checks must run in the aggregation service after all joins/aggregations and before any result is returned to caller (not only at gateway). This prevents joins or backfill artifacts from producing exposed values.
   - Ensure enforcement also runs for backfill/canary results (post‑backfill verification) and for any cached/async responses.
   - Attach tests demonstrating enforcement in aggregation codepath and post‑backfill verification outputs from staging.

7) Backfill/migration constraints (MUST)
   - Backfill must use encrypted temporary storage. External/public/analyst access to new indices must be disabled until canary validations pass and suppression checks confirmed.
   - Post‑backfill run an automated suppression re‑validation test and abort/backout if any cell violates effective_min.
   - Provide staging canary logs showing these steps (run 12355) and automated revert criteria in runbook.

8) Shared‑index + per‑tenant policy interplay (MUST)
   - Shared indices are acceptable only if per‑tenant cryptographic separation and tenant‑scoped auth are enforced. Required: per‑tenant key derivation or per‑tenant envelope encryption for pseudonyms, tenant‑scoped query authorization, and suppression computed per tenant before any cross‑tenant aggregation is returned.
   - If per‑tenant overrides are used on shared indices, prove via tests that no cross‑tenant inference is possible (attach multi‑tenant attack simulation results).

9) Monitoring & misuse alerts (MUST)
   - Add these concrete detection thresholds and wire them to on‑call:
     a) Alert if a principal makes >50 queries/hour returning cells within 2× effective_min (suspicious small‑cell activity).
     b) Alert if a principal issues >200 unique group‑by combinations in 60 minutes.
     c) Alert if a principal requests >5000 rows or attempts bulk exports in a short window.
   - When an alert fires, automated mitigation: enforce temporary throttle/quarantine of principal and create an incident ticket for Privacy & Security.
   - Provide monitoring dashboard links or staging alert demonstration logs.

10) KMS / pseudonymization (MUST)
   - Confirm per‑tenant key derivation is enabled when per‑tenant overrides exist (or prove threat model why not). If per‑tenant keying cannot be used, require additional protections (no overrides that reduce suppression, or per‑tenant index separation).
   - Provide key‑access audit logs and rotation evidence in PR.

11) CI & test evidence (MUST)
   - Provide CI links for unit 12352, integration 12353, full 12354 and staging 12355 demonstrating passing tests for: dynamic suppression enforcement, forbidden override rejection, post‑backfill suppression validation, and monitoring alert firing in staging. Attach these links to PR.

12) ARCH-77 updates (MUST)
   - Update ARCH‑77 with suppression policy format, override workflow, approval roles, secure config location, and runtime enforcement details. Link updated ARCH‑77 in PR.

Optional but recommended (non‑blocking)
- Consider limiting exposed group‑by dimensionality (max dims per request) and adding DP for externally published reports (epsilon <= 1, delta <= 1e‑5) if high sensitivity customers are served.
- Consider truncating HMAC outputs in logs for additional anti‑linkability.

Decision / next step
- I will grant full Responsible‑AI sign‑off once items 1–12 above are implemented and the CI/staging artifacts are attached to the PR (links to passing runs and sample audit entries). At that point I will send final StopRai.

Rationale
- Dynamic suppression is powerful but adds risk if overrides or storage/approval are not strictly controlled. The listed concrete constraints prevent accidental or privileged re‑identification and provide auditable governance.

Responsible AI review — conditional approval with required actions:

1) PII / data-governance risks (identify & mitigate)
- Likely revenue-related PII to minimize/encrypt/tokenize: customer/owner names, billing/shipping addresses, tax IDs, bank/account numbers, payment instrument details (even masked last4 must be treated carefully), invoice identifiers linked to individuals, email/phone, customer internal IDs if linkable to individuals, tenancy identifiers that map to a person.  
- Action: produce a PII inventory and data-flow diagram for /api/revenue within 5 business days. Mark each field: PII/non-PII, sensitivity, retention requirement, and required protection level.
- Action: apply field-level encryption or tokenization for sensitive fields at rest + TLS in transit; use vault-managed keys and rotate keys on schedule.

2) Logging, retention, and DSR (erasure) requirements
- Ensure centralized logging scrubs/redacts request/response bodies for any PII before persistence. Implement reject-by-default or mask-by-default logging for this endpoint.  
- Action: add automated redaction rules to pipeline, and test them in CI with sample PII payloads. Document retention windows and automated erasure flows; implement DSR pipeline to locate & delete personal records across DBs/logs/archives.

3) ML / automated decisioning risks
- If revenue or historical revenue is used for models, risks include leakage of PII, amplification of bias tied to socioeconomic signals, and re-identification from high-dimensional data.  
- Action: prohibit use of raw revenue-linked PII in model training. Instead, require aggregated, anonymized, or differentially-private transforms. For tests/migrations use synthetic or statistically similar non-production data.
- Action: run privacy assessment for any ML use (re-identification risk, membership inference), and apply differential privacy or safe aggregation when feasible.

4) Provenance, versioning, explainability, and audit
- Require dataset versioning (hash of extract/transforms), feature lineage, model versioning, and decision logs that record model id/version, input feature snapshot (IDs only, not PII), timestamp, and rationale/score.  
- Action: add model & feature metadata to the internal catalog (dataset id, extraction query, transform script, owner, timestamp); store decision audit logs with controlled retention and access controls.

5) Consent & legal considerations
- Confirm lawful basis for using revenue data in analytics or ML (consent, contract, legitimate interest); capture consent metadata and maintain it in a lookup accessible to data pipelines. For EU/UK customers ensure GDPR DSR workflows (access/erasure/portability) are implementable for revenue-derived records.  
- Action: legal/DP owner to sign off on permitted downstream uses before analytics or training begins.

6) Validate proposed mitigations and recommended additional controls
- The listed mitigations (authZ, schema validation, parameterized queries, vault secrets, SCA, scrubbed logs, distributed rate-limits) are necessary but not sufficient alone for Responsible AI. Additional required controls:  
  a) Data minimization policy (store only fields required for business).  
  b) No production PII in dev/staging; enforce masked or synthetic data in non-prod.  
  c) Quarterly access reviews and just-in-time approvals for sensitive dataset access; role-based least privilege.  
  d) Privacy-preserving training options (differential privacy, aggregation, synthetic data) for any ML using revenue features.  
  e) Automated tests in CI that validate log redaction, schema validation, and absence of raw PII in artifacts.  
  f) Model governance: fairness/bias checks, performance monitoring, drift detection, and rollout/rollback procedures.

7) Required architecture / operational changes
- Add a feature store or dataset catalog with RBAC and lineage support.  
- Implement centralized DLP/redaction at logging layer and ensure logs are immutable/auditable.  
- Consider tenant-isolation options: prefer per-tenant encryption keys or row-level encryption with tenant keying if whole-tenant data access must be prevented. If multi-tenant DB stays, enforce strict row-level authZ and encryption-in-flight for tenant-scoped extracts.  
- Create a DSR orchestration service to support erasure across DBs/logs/archives and ensure migrations respect erasure constraints.

8) Acceptance / block criteria (conditional proceed)
- Conditional approval to proceed to Merger only if the team provides:  
  a) PII inventory + data-flow and evidence of field-level protections (encryption/tokenization) for sensitive fields;  
  b) Logging redaction rules implemented & CI tests proving redaction;  
  c) Legal sign-off on permitted uses of revenue data and DSR compliance plan;  
  d) Confirmation that no production PII will be used in dev/staging (or that synthetic masked datasets are in use);  
  e) Plan and timeline for model governance artifacts (dataset versioning, decision logging) if ML will consume revenue data.  
- If any of the above are missing or not demonstrably addressed, block merging until remediations are completed.

Summary recommendation: do not merge to production until the short checklist above (PII inventory, redaction, legal consent sign-off, non-prod data controls, and CI redaction tests) is completed; once done, the Responsible AI reviewer can pass final sign-off.

label: ToMerger
payload:
Responsible AI detailed disposition for items 1–12 (per-Item A: disposition / B: required changes / C: required evidence / D: re-review):

1) AuthN/AuthZ & API surface
A: Needs Design Change — server-side enforcement required plus scope-to-field mapping for data access.
B: Enforce RBAC/ABAC checks in service layer (not only gateway); annotate OpenAPI with scopes per route and per-field access rules; implement separation-of-duty controls for admin/impersonation endpoints; require just-in-time elevated access logging.
C: Evidence: OpenAPI excerpt with scopes, unit/integration tests exercising authZ matrix (role/tenant combos), audit log showing admin/impersonation calls, threat-model note on least-privilege mappings.
D: Yes — Arch & Security re-review after fixes.
Acceptance test: automated authZ matrix tests that assert forbidden for unauthorized combinations and allowed for valid ones.
Impact: minimal latency; adds complexity to policy management.

2) Tenant isolation & per-tenant keys
A: Needs Design Change (Blocker for analytics/feature-store use until resolved)
B: Adopt per-tenant keying or tenant-scoped tokenization for sensitive identifiers destined for feature stores; if per-tenant CMKs are infeasible, enforce strong logical isolation (row-level encryption with tenant-bound keys) and separate feature-store namespaces per-tenant.
C: Evidence: key-policy docs, KMS logs showing tenant CMK creation, demo of query/access using tenant keying, architecture diagram showing feature-store separation.
D: Yes — Arch re-review required.
Acceptance test: attempt cross-tenant access from analytics job should be denied; crypto audit proving tenant keys cannot decrypt other tenant data.
Impact: possible query latency and key-management overhead; mitigate with cache of wrapped keys and asynchronous re-keying.

3) Encryption at rest/in transit & DB migrations
A: Needs Design Change
B: Ensure field-level encryption for PII before any export to analytics/feature stores; in migrations include transforms that preserve encryption or produce tokenized outputs; do not place plaintext PII into backups or intermediate artifacts. Document which fields are queryable and risks of reconstruction.
C: Evidence: migration scripts with transform steps, encryption-at-rest config, sample backup audits proving no plaintext, test demonstrating queryability vs reconstruction limits.
D: Security re-review after fixes.
Acceptance test: automated scan of migration artifacts/backups for plaintext PII; penetration test on encrypted-but-queryable fields to show inability to reconstruct raw PII.
Impact: may restrict some query patterns; consider envelope encryption and searchable encryption trade-offs.

4) Key management and rotation
A: Needs Design Change
B: Define rotation policy that preserves reproducibility: either version datasets with key-ids, support re-encryption pipelines, and document impact on models (hash/version metadata). Implement key rollover tests and emergency rollback plan.
C: Evidence: KMS rotation policy, logs of rotation events, test demonstrating re-encryption/replay of training dataset and model reproducibility metadata.
D: Security re-review required.
Acceptance test: simulated rotation that triggers re-encryption flow and shows model re-training or documented migration path; artifact showing key-id tied to dataset versions.
Impact: rotation may require re-encrypt/retrain; mitigate with metadata and selective re-encryption windows.

5) DSR/erasure across replicas & archives
A: Blocker until erasure propagation is demonstrable
B: Implement DSR orchestration that orchestrates erasure from primary DB, feature stores, analytics snapshots, model training corpora, backups, and logs; pipelines must track derived data lineage to locate derived artifacts for erasure.
C: Evidence: DSR playbook, automated erasure test runs removing a synthetic user from DB -> feature store -> models, logs of deletions, and feature-store erasure demo.
D: Yes — Arch & Security re-review after remediation.
Acceptance test: end-to-end DSR test that proves removal of sample PII from all stores and that model training pipelines either exclude erased records or are retrained/annotated.
Impact: potential need for model retraining or incremental retrain strategies; plan for availability impact during mass erasures.

6) Logging, redaction, and retention
A: Needs Design Change
B: Enforce redact-before-write at logging ingest; implement DLP rules for telemetry and block forwarding unredacted payloads to analytics; retention policies and automated purge for logs and telemetry with audit trail.
C: Evidence: log pipeline config, CI redaction tests with sample PII, logs demonstrating redaction prior to persistence, retention policy docs.
D: Security re-review suggested.
Acceptance test: CI test that injects PII sample and asserts the persisted log contains only masked values; audit of retention purge runs.
Impact: negligible latency; ensure redaction rules are performant and centrally maintained.

7) OpenAPI, input validation, and injection risks
A: Acceptable with hardening
B: Enforce strict OpenAPI schema validation and reject unknown fields; validate numeric ranges and types for revenue features; sanitize/normalize inputs to reduce poisoning vectors; add ingestion-side sanity checks and anomaly detection for outliers.
C: Evidence: OpenAPI schemas, CI tests validating invalid/poisoned payload rejects, anomaly-detection alerts tuning docs.
D: Security re-check recommended.
Acceptance test: supply malformed/poisoned payloads in CI and assert rejection and logged incident.
Impact: helps robustness; anomaly checks may add compute but can be sampled.

8) Rate limiting, DoS, and abuse mitigation
A: Needs Design Change
B: Add per-tenant and per-principal rate limits, quota enforcement for analytics ingestion, and telemetry quotas for model-feature updates; throttle large/batch ingestion that could poison models. Log and alert on abnormal ingestion patterns and provide replay controls.
C: Evidence: rate-limit config, simulated DoS/ingest tests, alerting rules and dashboards.
D: Security re-review suggested.
Acceptance test: stress test showing limits enforced and no silent ingestion into feature store.
Impact: possible increased latency or throttling; provide backpressure handling and client error codes.

9) CI/CD, secrets handling, and dependency management
A: Needs Design Change
B: Prevent secrets in artifacts; ensure ML artifacts do not contain KMS plaintexts; include SBOMs for model libs; SCA for ML dependencies; block builds with known risky deps. Ensure CI does not leak PII into logs/artifacts.
C: Evidence: CI pipeline logs sanitized, SBOMs, SCA scan reports, secrets-scan proof, artifact inspection showing no plaintext secrets.
D: Security re-review required.
Acceptance test: CI run that fails on secret detection or known vuln deps; artifact audit showing no secret leakage.
Impact: small CI complexity; mitigate via automated scans and gating.

10) DSR/DSR test automation and verification
A: Blocker until automated DSR verification exists for feature stores and archived training sets
B: Implement automated DSR test harness that triggers a synthetic erasure and verifies removal across stores and artifacts; schedule periodic DSR verification runs and audit logs for regulators.
C: Evidence: automated test runs, pass/fail reports, logs of deletion operations, attestation report.
D: Yes — Arch/Security re-review after implementation.
Acceptance test: scheduled DSR test run that proves end-to-end deletion and provides signed attestation.
Impact: test runs may involve reprocessing; schedule during off-peak windows.

11) ML/analytics & feature stores
A: Needs Design Change
B: Enforce feature-store policies: lineage metadata, PII tokenization/encryption of features, exposure of only aggregated/DP versions for cross-tenant analytics, retention & erasure semantics for derived features, and decision-logging for models. Require synthetic/differential-privacy for tests/migrations where PII would otherwise be used.
C: Evidence: feature-store metadata records, lineage traces, tokenization demo, DP parameter config used for aggregations, decision-log samples with model id/version and non-PII feature snapshot, synthetic-data generation tests.
D: Yes — Arch re-review required.
Acceptance test: feature lineage query demonstrates origin for a derived feature; DP aggregation unit tests verifying epsilon setting and noise characteristics; erasure of base features removes derived features per policy.
Impact: DP/noise affects accuracy; recommend tuning epsilon and using large-cohort aggregations; per-tenant keys affect join performance—mitigate with pre-computed aggregates.

12) Evidence requested from Author/QA
A: Needs Design Change (if any requested artifacts are missing)
B: Provide missing artifacts: migration demo with masking, KMS policy & logs, CI pipeline runs proving redaction, DSR test runs, OpenAPI excerpts with scopes, raw SQL usage report.
C: Evidence: the artifacts themselves, plus passing test runs and signed attestations from Data Protection/Legal.
D: Arch & Security re-review after submission.
Acceptance test: checklist of artifacts present and automated tests passing.

Blockers summary (RAI-critical):
- Item 5 (DSR/erasure across replicas & archives): Blocker until end-to-end erasure demonstrable.
- Item 10 (DSR test automation): Blocker until automated verification exists.
- Item 2 (Tenant isolation & per-tenant keys): Blocker for any cross-tenant analytics or model training that could leak PII; minimal remediation required.

Minimal remediation per blocker (quick steps):
- DSR: implement orchestration to propagate deletions, run end-to-end test on synthetic subject, and provide logs/attestation (Operational; Security+QA re-review).
- DSR test automation: add CI job that runs synthetic erasure and verifies downstream stores; produce test report (Operational; Arch/Security re-review).
- Tenant isolation: at minimum, tokenization/envelope encryption for feature-store exports scoped per-tenant; provide key-policy and demo (Architectural; Arch re-review).

Prioritized checklist (high->low):
1) Implement automated DSR test and run end-to-end deletion (High risk — Blocker — re-review required).
2) Ensure tenant isolation/tokenization for analytics/feature-store exports (High risk — Blocker for ML use — re-review).
3) Prove logging redaction via CI tests (High risk — Needs Design Change — Security re-review).
4) Add authZ matrix tests and scope annotations in OpenAPI (Medium risk — Needs Design Change).
5) Add per-tenant and per-principal rate limits + abuse-detection (Medium risk).
6) KMS rotation policy, re-encryption plan, and reproducibility docs (Medium risk).
7) Feature-store lineage, DP/aggregation config for analytics, and decision-logging (Medium risk — Architectural changes).
8) CI/CD secrets & SBOM enforcement (Low/Medium risk).
9) Input validation/poisoning controls and anomaly detection (Low risk).

Suggested acceptance criteria (explicit checks/tests):
- End-to-end DSR CI test pass (remove sample user -> verify deletion across DB, feature store, analytics snapshots, models/logs).
- CI redaction test: sample PII in request -> persisted logs contain masked values only.
- Tenant isolation test: cross-tenant decrypt attempt fails; analytics job cannot join raw PII across tenants.
- Feature-lineage query returns provenance chain; decision log contains model id/version and non-PII input snapshot.
- DP aggregation unit tests with documented epsilon and statistical impact report.
- AuthZ matrix tests pass for all role/tenant combinations.

Privacy-preserving technique recommendations (practical):
- Use tokenization/envelope encryption for per-tenant sensitive fields; keep wrapped keys in KMS.
- For analytics, expose DP aggregates (Laplace/Gaussian noise) with epsilon tuned per use-case; require minimum cohort sizes for DP to apply.
- Generate synthetic datasets (GANs or stat-sim) for dev/staging and migrations; certify via privacy metric (distance/utility tradeoff).
- Apply selective differential privacy for training where needed; otherwise use aggregated features or feature-binning to reduce re-identification risk.

Scalability/availability impacts and mitigations
- Per-tenant CMKs: additional key ops can affect latency — mitigate with wrapped-key caching and async decryption for non-latency-critical jobs.
- DP/noise: reduces analytical accuracy — mitigate via cohort sizing and mixing DP with large-scale aggregation.
- DSR automation: may require reprocessing or model retrain; schedule during maintenance windows and provide stale/validity tags for models until retrain completes.

Final disposition: Conditional approval to continue code review but block merging to production until Blocker items (2,5,10) and CI redaction tests (item 6/12 evidence) are demonstrably resolved. Provide the requested artifacts and automated test reports; RAI will re-review after fixes. 

Next steps for Arch/Security/Author: deliver the DSR automation run, tenant keying/tokenization demo, CI redaction/test runs, and updated OpenAPI/authZ tests. Once provided, Responsible AI will re-evaluate and either move to Acceptable or identify remaining gaps.

payload:
Responsible-AI concise per-item assessment for PR #1234 — items 1–11 (A–F). Blockers: items 1,4,10. Required explicit CI tests named for verification are included.

1) Per-tenant KMS topology / tenant_keying_test
A: Blocker (for any analytics/feature-store use exposing tenant-sensitive fields).
B: Minimal remediation: implement per-tenant envelope-keying (tenant CMKs or tenant-wrapped data keys) OR strong logical separation (separate feature-store namespaces + tenant-bound wrapped keys). Provide key-policy per-tenant and access controls limiting decrypt to tenant-scoped services.
C: Evidence/artifacts: KMS key-policy doc; CI job tenant_keying_test; test steps: (CI job name: tenant_keying_test) create sample record with tenantA, export to feature-store, attempt decrypt with tenantB key -> expected: decrypt fails (error/403). Logs: KMS access logs showing only tenantA principal used. Sample input/expected output: create payload {tenantId: A, revenue: X, tok: ...} -> feature-store contains encrypted blob; cross-tenant decrypt attempt returns unauthorized.
D: Yes — Arch re-review after fixes.
E: Techniques: envelope encryption + tokenization; keep wrapped keys in KMS and return only wrapped keys to services. If analytics require cross-tenant aggregates, expose DP aggregates only. Parameter suggestions: use AES-GCM-256 for content keys; KMS RSA/ECC per tenant for wrapping; caching wrapped-key metadata with TTL 5 minutes.
F: Perf/availability: per-tenant key ops add latency. Mitigation: cache wrapped keys in a secure cache; pre-warm keys for batch jobs; async decrypt for non-latency-critical pipelines.

2) Key rotation & re-encryption plan
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: document rotation policy mapping key-ids to dataset versions; implement re-encryption pipeline or use versioned encryption metadata so datasets record key-id used; provide rollback plan for failed rotation.
C: Evidence: CI job rotation_replay_test. Test: rotate key for tenantA, run rotation_reencrypt_job -> expected: dataset records show new key-id; replay training job (rotation_replay_test) uses key-id metadata to fetch correct wrapped key and reproduces model input hashes within tolerance. Logs: rotation events in KMS + re-encryption job success trace.
D: Yes — Security re-review after fixes.
E: Techniques: include key-id in dataset manifest; prefer lazy re-encryption for cold data. No DP change here.
F: Perf: re-encryption heavy; mitigate via batched background jobs and rate-limit re-encrypt operations.

3) DB migrations & backups
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: ensure migration scripts never materialize plaintext to disk; use streaming transforms that encrypt on-write; avoid writing plaintext to temp files/logs. For indexed/searchable fields, use deterministic tokenization where necessary but document reconstruction risk.
C: Evidence: CI job encrypt_columns_migration_scan. Acceptance: run migration demo (script name: migrate_encrypt_demo) on synthetic DB -> then run no_plaintext_scan (artifact) -> expected: zero plaintext matches. Provide migration script, pre/post checksums, and backup scan results.
D: Security re-review after fixes.
E: Techniques: envelope encryption; deterministic tokenization only when necessary for joins (document K-anonymity risks). For indexed fields, prefer tokenized indexes (hashed with tenant salt) not raw encryption that allows reconstruction.
F: Perf: deterministic tokens can enable index usage but risk linkage; randomized encryption prevents searches — compensate with precomputed indexes or tokenized join keys.

4) DSR orchestration coverage (erasure_e2e_test)
A: Blocker (must be demonstrable end-to-end before approving). 
B: Minimal remediation: implement a DSR orchestration service that executes deletion across primary DB, replicas, backups (or marks for purge), search indices, feature stores, analytic snapshots, and third-party exports; include lineage mapping to locate derived data. Implement blocking/retrain policy for models referencing removed records.
C: Evidence: CI job erasure_e2e_test. Test script: create synthetic subject SID_X -> ingest through /api/revenue -> run dsr_delete(SID_X) -> verify: primary DB row removed or flagged; replica sync shows deletion/flag; backups show redaction or scheduled purge record; feature-store remove/mark derived features; analytic snapshots removed/annotated; model retrain/process either excludes SID_X or provides audit entry. Expected outputs: deletion logs, audit attestation (signed), and feature-store deletion confirmation. Provide timeline SLA for propagation.
D: Yes — Arch & Security re-review after remediation.
E: Techniques: lineage metadata to trace derived data; for models, prefer flagging and incremental retrain or record-level masking. No DP parameter change here, but use synthetic replays for verification.
F: Perf: large-scale erasures/retains may require model retrain; mitigate by scheduled maintenance windows and incremental retraining strategies.

5) Logging/redaction pipeline placement (redaction_pipeline_test)
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: move redaction to earliest ingestion point (API gateway or logging ingest) so no downstream system receives unredacted payloads. Implement DLP rules that block/purge unredacted flows and ensure logbackends only accept sanitized events.
C: Evidence: CI job redaction_pipeline_test. Test: send request with sample PII -> validate persisted logs (CI asserts) contain masked fields only; check pipeline ordering proof (diagram) showing redaction before feature-store sink. Provide examples: input {email: e@x.com} -> persisted log {email: "[REDACTED]"}.
D: Security re-review suggested.
E: Techniques: structured logging + automatic schema-based redactors; tokenization for features that need linked identifiers. Parameter: mask replacements keep last 2 chars for debugging only if allowed by policy.
F: Perf: negligible; ensure redaction rules are compiled/optimized and centrally versioned.

6) AuthN/AuthZ enforcement locus (authz_matrix_test)
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: enforce server-side RBAC/ABAC in service layer with OpenAPI scope annotations mapped to runtime policy engine; require separation-of-duty for admin/impersonation flows and JIT approvals for elevated access.
C: Evidence: CI job authz_matrix_test. Test: matrix of role/tenant combinations -> expected: only permitted role+tenant combos succeed; provide OpenAPI excerpt mapping scopes to endpoints. Logs: audit trail of impersonation with justification token.
D: Yes — Arch & Security re-review after fixes.
E: Techniques: use centralized policy engine (e.g., OPA) with per-field policies. No DP change.
F: Perf: small added latency for policy checks; mitigate with policy-cache layer.

7) Rate-limiting & abuse mitigation (rate_limit_attack_sim)
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: implement per-tenant and per-principal rate limits, ingestion quotas, throttles for batch updates, and anomaly detectors that can quarantine suspicious inputs before reaching feature stores. Include circuit-breaker patterns for extreme surge.
C: Evidence: CI job rate_limit_attack_sim. Test: simulate high-rate ingestion -> expected: 429/blocked after threshold; confirm quarantined payloads not ingested to feature-store. Provide config: per-tenant RPS, burst tokens, quotas per day.
D: Security re-review suggested.
E: Techniques: ingest sampling + anomaly scoring; for high-risk feeds, route to quarantine and manual review. No DP specifics.
F: Perf: throttling can affect availability for heavy clients; recommend backpressure/error codes and retry guidance.

8) Raw SQL & queryability trade-offs (raw_sql_audit)
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: audit raw SQL occurrences and parameterize all queries; block any migration that writes plaintext PII to analytics/feature-store; document searchable-field design (tokenization/hashes) and proof that encrypted-but-queryable fields cannot be reconstructed.
C: Evidence: raw_sql_audit artifact listing occurrences; CI job raw_sql_audit_run producing report; code walkthrough session log. Acceptance: raw_sql_audit_run returns zero unparameterized PII-writes to analytics sinks.
D: Security re-review required.
E: Techniques: use keyed-hash tokens for joinable keys; avoid reversible searchable encryption unless necessary and documented. If using deterministic tokens, add tenant-salt to avoid cross-tenant linkage.
F: Perf: hashed joins fast; reversible encryption with searchable features slower; mitigate via precomputed indices.

9) Serialization/deserialization risks (deserialization_safety_test)
A: Acceptable with remediation
B: Minimal remediation: ban unsafe serializers (e.g., native pickling), enforce safe JSON/YAML parsers, add input schema validation and size limits; add CI SAST/PR checks to flag risky deps or unsafe patterns.
C: Evidence: SAST report + CI job deserialization_safety_test which loads representative payloads and asserts no unsafe class instantiation. Provide unit tests that deserialize allowed schema only.
D: Security re-review suggested.
E: Techniques: strict schema validation; limit allowed data types and avoid arbitrary code-execution capable serializers.
F: Perf: negligible.

10) Cross-system DSR for ML/analytics (feature_lineage_erasure_test)
A: Blocker (must demonstrate that derived features and models honor erasure semantics automatically or via documented retrain path).
B: Minimal remediation: extend DSR orchestration to include feature-store lineage mapping and model artifact indexes; ensure feature-store supports record deletion or tombstoning plus derived-feature removal or model retrain blocking. Add automation: when DSR occurs, either remove derived features or mark models for retrain and prevent inferencing for affected users until resolved.
C: Evidence: CI job feature_lineage_erasure_test. Test steps: ingest SID_X -> compute derived features -> train model -> perform dsr_delete(SID_X) -> verify derived features removed/marked and model logs show affected model flagged for retrain or contain annotation that inference excludes SID_X. Provide lineage traces and model re-eval artifacts.
D: Yes — Arch & Security re-review after fixes.
E: Techniques: store lineage metadata at ingestion (source record id -> derived feature ids). Use DP for published aggregates to reduce need for deletions. For testing, generate synthetic datasets.
F: Perf: lineage storage increases metadata size; maintain efficient indices and retention policies.

11) CI/CD placement for redaction & no-prod-PII gates (ci_redaction_gate)
A: Needs Design Change
B: Minimal remediation: add CI gating jobs that detect PII in artifacts and block promotion to non-prod/prod; integrate synthetic data generator into CI and require it for any pipeline that uses production-like payloads. Ensure gates cannot be bypassed (enforce via branch protection and CI policy).
C: Evidence: CI job names ci_redaction_gate and ci_no_prod_pii_check. Tests: inject sample PII into build -> job fails. Provide sample artifact scans and proof that dev/stage datasets are synthetic or masked.
D: Security re-review required.
E: Techniques: synthetic data creation (stat-sim or GAN) with privacy metric thresholds (e.g., maximum record similarity < 0.2 measured by chosen metric). For analytics tests use DP-aggregates instead of raw data.
F: Perf: CI runtime increases; mitigate by sampling and targeted test suites.

Overall prioritized checklist (High->Low) and re-review guidance:
1) (High) Implement and demonstrate DSR orchestration + erasure_e2e_test (items 4 & 10) — Blocker — Arch & Security re-review.
2) (High) Implement per-tenant keying and tenant_keying_test (item 1) — Blocker — Arch re-review.
3) (High) CI redaction pipeline tests (item 5 & 11) — Needs Design Change — Security re-review.
4) (Medium) AuthZ matrix tests & OpenAPI mapping (item 6) — Needs Design Change — Arch/Security re-review.
5) (Medium) Key rotation/replay tests (item 2) — Needs Design Change — Security re-review.
6) (Medium) Feature-store lineage + feature_lineage_erasure_test (item 10/11) — Needs Design Change — Arch re-review.
7) (Medium) Raw SQL audit & migration scans (item 3 & 8) — Needs Design Change — Security re-review.
8) (Low) Deserialization SAST/unit tests (item 9) — Acceptable after simple fixes — Security re-check.
9) (Low) Rate limiting & abuse tests (item 7) — Needs Design Change — Security re-check.

Explicit acceptance tests (commands / CI job names):
- tenant_keying_test (CI): create tenantA record -> verify decrypt with tenantB fails
- rotation_replay_test (CI): rotate key -> reencrypt -> replay training job -> verify model inputs match pre-rotation hashes
- encrypt_columns_migration_scan (CI): run migration -> no_plaintext_scan -> pass
- erasure_e2e_test (CI): dsr_delete synthetic -> verify deletes across DB/replicas/backups/feature-store/analytics
- redaction_pipeline_test (CI): send PII -> persisted logs masked
- authz_matrix_test (CI): run role/tenant matrix -> expected allow/deny
- rate_limit_attack_sim (CI): simulated burst -> 429 enforced
- raw_sql_audit_run (CI): returns zero unparameterized PII writes
- deserialization_safety_test (CI): attempt unsafe payloads -> rejected
- feature_lineage_erasure_test (CI): derived features removed or model flagged
- ci_redaction_gate (CI): artifact scan fails if PII present

Summary disposition: conditional continuation of review allowed, but merge to production MUST be blocked until Blocker items (1,4,10) are demonstrably satisfied and CI acceptance tests above pass. After artifacts and CI test runs are provided, RAI will re-review and provide final Acceptable/Needs Design Change/Blocker verdicts.
